title: 👻 The Séance Engine: Finding the Ghost in the Data with TabPFN & Gemma
summary:
🕯️ The idea

What does your computer do while you sleep?

Mine is supposed to do almost nothing. CPU in single digits, a few kilobytes of network, "System Idle" all night long. So when I pictured a ghost living inside a machine, I didn't imagine a skull on the screen. I imagined one row in a boring log file that shouldn't be there.

The Séance Engine reads a day of ordinary system logs, asks an open tabular foundation model which moment is the hardest to believe, and then hands that moment to a local LLM. The LLM, playing the Spirit of the Machine, tells us what passed through the circuits in a short Día de los Muertos style story.

It finds the ghost in the data, then gives it a voice.

⚙️ How it works

Everything runs on my laptop: one Python file, about 100 lines.

1. The haunted log. 24 hourly rows of hour, cpu_usage, memory_usage and network_io_mb. By day it's VS Code; by night, idle. You can also point it at your own CSV: python seance_engine.py my_logs.csv.

2. The divination (TabPFN by Prior Labs). TabPFN is a classifier, and an anomaly detector needs a sense of what's "normal". So I used a small density-ratio trick:

  • For each row, hold it out.
  • Show TabPFN the other 23 real rows labelled real, next to random noise spread across the same range labelled noise.
  • Ask: how real does the held-out row look?

Ordinary hours score between 0.66 and 0.99. The witching hour scored this:

2026-10-29 02:33:00    8%   4 MB/s   System Idle       p_real 0.992
2026-10-29 03:33:00   98% 850 MB/s   UNKNOWN_PROCESS   p_real 0.006
2026-10-29 04:33:00    7%   5 MB/s   System Idle       p_real 0.992

Because hour is a feature, TabPFN isn't just flagging "big numbers". It learned that this machine sleeps at 3 AM, so 98% CPU at that hour is what doesn't fit. No training loop, no tuning: TabPFN does all of it in context.

3. The séance (Gemma 2 9B through Ollama). The anomalous row, including its p_real score, goes into a prompt that asks Gemma to speak as a gossipy, theatrical ghost who lives in the laptop's fan (fun, quirky, and chilling by the last line). Output streams to the terminal word by word, which feels a lot like a candle flickering.

4. The tracing (Sentry). The whole investigation is one Sentry trace, with spans for loading the logs, the TabPFN scan and the Gemma chat. Token counts go on the chat span.

The trace showed me something I didn't expect: the leave-one-out TabPFN scan (24 small fits on CPU) took 38 seconds, and Gemma took about a minute. The ghost costs more to find than to listen to.

👻 What the machine confessed

⚠️ ANOMALY DETECTED at 2026-10-29 03:33:00 (P(real)=0.006)

Ah, three thirty-three in the morning, that's when the veil thins, darlings! The fan whirred like a disco ball under a mariachi band as 98% of my beloved CPU hummed with the impossible, a process so shrouded, so strange, it registered as "UNKNOWN_PROCESS" on the logs. I saw it all, you see, every pixel flicker as 95% of the memory churned, a ghostly green glow illuminating its form. It downloaded a single video at 850 MB/s, a pixelated rendition of a chihuahua wearing a sombrero, its tiny paws drumming on a maraca. A forgotten relic, perhaps, from a life lived before this one. Now, the screen rests dark, the chihuahua frozen mid-shake, a reminder of that fleeting connection. Is it ever truly gone?

Every run summons a different visitor. The prompt asks Gemma for a gossipy ghost who lives in the laptop fan: give the ghost a petty hobby and one oddly specific detail, weave in every real number, and end on one quiet line that makes you glance at your own laptop.

💡 Why open models

  • The data stays home. These are behaviour logs from a personal machine. With open weights, TabPFN and Gemma both run locally, and nothing leaves the laptop. It works with Wi-Fi off.
  • I own the voice. I set the system prompt and the temperature, and I can swap models freely (MODEL = "gemma2:9b" is one line).
  • Free to haunt every night. A ghost should be ambient. Running a local check on last night's logs every morning costs nothing per call.
  • It runs on old hardware. This was built on an Intel Mac stuck on PyTorch 2.2. The newest TabPFN wouldn't install, but tabpfn==2.0.9 worked, and that's the point of open weights: you pick a version that fits the machine you actually have.

🛠️ Run it yourself 

ollama pull gemma2:9b
pip install -r requirements.txt   # tabpfn==2.0.9, numpy<2, pandas, ollama, sentry-sdk
python seance_engine.py
# optional tracing
SENTRY_DSN="your-dsn" python seance_engine.py

🔗 Links

  • Code: https://github.com/Prekshabarjatya/seance-engine
  • TabPFN: https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN
  • Gemma: https://ai.google.dev/gemma
  • Ollama: https://ollama.com
  • Sentry: https://sentry.io

Happy Día de los Muertos. Leave a candle on for your machines tonight. 🕯️

title: I Built a VS Code Extension That Shows What Changed Since Your Last Save (No Git Needed)
summary:
| SavePoint Diff adds live gutter markers and a Source Control panel for your unsaved edits, in any folder, Git repo or not.

Open a file in VS Code inside a Git repo and you get those handy colored bars in the gutter. Green for added, blue for modified, red for deleted.

Now open a scratch script, a config folder, or a project you never ran git init on. Nothing. You're editing blind.

That's why I built SavePoint Diff.

What it does

It shows what you've changed since your last save, live, on every keystroke:

  • 🟢 Green = added lines
  • 🔵 Blue = modified lines
  • 🔴 Red = deleted-line markers

It also adds a SavePoint Diff entry to the Source Control panel listing every open file with unsaved changes, with a Save All button at the top and a save icon per file. Click any file and VS Code's native split diff opens: last-saved version on the left, your live editable buffer on the right.

No setup

  • No .git folder required
  • No network access
  • No account, no telemetry, no external services

Install it, open a file, start typing. Markers appear immediately and clear the moment you save.

Other bits I'm happy with

  • "M" badges on changed files in the Explorer and on editor tabs
  • Per-change revert: hover a gutter marker and click "↺ Revert this change"
  • Live status bar tally: SavePoint: ON +12 ~4 -2

Try it 

ext install StayElite.StayElite-Savepoint-Diff

Paste that into Quick Open (Ctrl+P), or grab it from the Marketplace. It's MIT licensed and the source is on GitHub.

If you try it, I'd love to hear what's missing. Issues and ideas are very welcome.

title: UIDesignRequiresCompatibility ends with the iOS 27 SDK: finding the code that paints over Liquid Glass
summary:
When iOS 26 introduced Liquid Glass, many teams added one key to Info.plist and moved on: UIDesignRequiresCompatibility, set to YES, keeps the earlier design. Apple's page for the key always called it temporary ("Temporarily use this key while reviewing and refining your app's UI"), and now it has an end date in practice: "The system ignores this key when you build for iOS 27 or later."

The SDK you build with is not entirely your choice. App Store submissions says that starting April 2027, iOS apps uploaded to App Store Connect "must be built with the iOS & iPadOS 27 SDK or later". Today the Upcoming Requirements page still asks for the iOS 26 SDK, so this is a planning item, not an emergency.

Deleting the key is one line. The real work is finding where your own code fights the new bars.

What actually needs review

Apple's Adopting Liquid Glass puts it this way: custom backgrounds and appearances in bars "might overlay or interfere with Liquid Glass". In a typical UIKit app that has been around since iOS 15, that code looks like this (from the test fixture I use below):

let navigation = UINavigationBarAppearance()
navigation.configureWithOpaqueBackground()
navigation.backgroundColor = .harborNavy
navigation.shadowColor = .clear
UINavigationBar.appearance().standardAppearance = navigation
UINavigationBar.appearance().scrollEdgeAppearance = navigation

let tabs = UITabBarAppearance()
tabs.configureWithOpaqueBackground()
tabs.backgroundColor = .white
UITabBar.appearance().isTranslucent = false

UIToolbar.appearance().barTintColor = .harborNavy

None of this is wrong; it is a brand decision made for an older design. With the opt-out ignored, it sits on top of a material the system wants to draw.

Listing it with glassready

I wrote an open-source CLI, glassready, that reads a native iOS, Flutter or React Native/Expo project and lists the opt-out and these places. It does not build, run or change anything. On the native-uikit-optout fixture from its repository:

npx @mcamdali/glassready

Excerpt of today's output (glassready 0.1.3, rules liquid-glass@2026.10.27, exit code 1):

Harbor · native iOS · .
target Harbor: opts out of Liquid Glass (Harbor/Info.plist)

The Liquid Glass opt-out is ignored when built with the iOS 27 SDK; 4 custom styles to review first

ERROR    GLS001 Liquid Glass opt-out that the iOS 27 SDK ignores
         Harbor/Info.plist:42
WARNING  GLS002 Bar appearance with its own background
         Harbor/AppDelegate.swift:28
WARNING  GLS002 Bar appearance with its own background
         Harbor/AppDelegate.swift:38
WARNING  GLS003 Bar colour or translucency set the old way
         Harbor/AppDelegate.swift:42
WARNING  GLS003 Bar colour or translucency set the old way
         Harbor/AppDelegate.swift:44
INFO     GLS006 Blur layer without a Liquid Glass counterpart
         Harbor/PortMapViewController.swift:5
INFO     GLS008 Fixed bar height or safe-area arithmetic
         Harbor/PortMapViewController.swift:26
         A number added to the safe-area insets.

1 error, 4 warnings, 2 info

The last finding is the subtle one. The fixture places a panel 49 points above the bottom safe area, the height of the classic tab bar:

summary.bottomAnchor.constraint(
    equalTo: view.bottomAnchor, constant: -(view.safeAreaInsets.bottom + 49)),

The report's fix: constrain to safeAreaLayoutGuide instead of adding a bar height, do not read the tab bar's frame for layout, and check the screen with the tab bar minimized as well.

The fixes the report gives

Each finding names a fix. For the bars, condensed from the report:

  • Opaque appearances (GLS002): remove configureWithOpaqueBackground() and the background and shadow settings, or apply them only before iOS 26 with if #available(iOS 26.0, *). Move the brand colour to tintColor and the title text attributes.
  • barTintColor, isTranslucent = false (GLS003): remove them, or keep them only for earlier versions; use tintColor for the bar's buttons.
  • Blur layers (GLS006): behind a floating panel, use UIGlassEffect on iOS 26 and later and keep the blur as the fallback; over a photo or a map, keep it.

The repository also has the same app after these fixes. The report on it:

target Harbor: no opt-out (Harbor/Info.plist)

Ready for Liquid Glass: no opt-out and no custom bar styles found
Impact: none (0 of 100)
Already uses: UIGlassEffect

0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 info

React Native, Expo and Flutter

In React Native the opt-out sits in ios//Info.plist; in Expo it can sit in ios.infoPlist in app.json. On the React Native 0.88.1 fixture (native stack around JavaScript bottom tabs), glassready reports, among others:

WARNING  GLS101 Native stack header with its own background
         App.tsx:54
         headerStyle.backgroundColor paints the header.
INFO     GLS102 Tab bar drawn in JavaScript
         App.tsx:29
         createBottomTabNavigator draws the tab bar in JavaScript.

The rule data explains the second one: a JavaScript tab bar "keeps its look" with the iOS 27 SDK while the native headers and sheets around it become Liquid Glass. For Flutter, the rules flag Cupertino bars that Flutter draws itself and UiKitView platform views next to Flutter widgets.

What the simulator showed

The repository records a simulator comparison from 27 October 2026, which I did not repeat here: the same UIKit app built with Xcode 27.1, with and without the key. On iOS 27.0 the screenshots match, so the key is ignored; on iOS 26.4 they differ. While the key stays, one build shows two designs depending on the device.

Limitations

From the README, and they matter:

  • Patterns, not a compiler. The rules are regular expressions over source text with comments and strings blanked. Generated code, macros or unusual shapes can be missed or matched by mistake.
  • Only the app's own sources. Pods, Swift packages outside the app folder, node_modules and Flutter plugins are not read.
  • .xcconfig files are not read; app.config.js/.ts are read as text, not run.
  • A warning is not a verdict. A brand colour on a bar can be a deliberate decision; the warning says where the code paints over the bar. Look at the screen on an iOS 27 simulator and decide.
  • The impact score sorts projects; in the README's words, "it does not grade the design."

Try it

In your app folder (Node.js 22.12 or later):

npx @mcamdali/glassready
npx @mcamdali/glassready --fail-on error --format markdown --output glassready.md

The second writes a Markdown report for a pull request and fails only on the ignored opt-out (exit 1 on the fixture above).

The opt-out answers how the app will look. Whether it will launch at all with the same SDK is a separate check, covered in "Built with the iOS 27 SDK, a UIKit app without a scene stops at launch".

Repository: github.com/muhittincamdali/glassready (MIT).

Muhittin Camdali is a mobile engineer (iOS, Flutter, React Native) and the author of glassready.

title: How AI Assistants Decide Which Dev Tool to Recommend (and How to Be the One They Pick)
summary:
Think about the last time you picked a library. There's a good chance you didn't Google "best Node.js queue library." You asked ChatGPT, Claude or your editor's assistant, got three names, and tried the first one.

That moment, when an assistant chooses which three names to list, is now one of the most important distribution channels for developer tools. And most maintainers have never looked at it.

This post covers where those recommendations come from, how to measure yours with a ~40-line script, and the changes that actually move them.

Two kinds of answer, two sources of truth

When a developer asks for a recommendation, the assistant answers in one of two modes:

Mode When it happens Where the answer comes from
From memory Coding assistants, chats without web search, quick questions What the model learned in training, up to its knowledge cutoff
From search ChatGPT search, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, Claude with web search Live retrieval: search indexes (Bing, Google, their own), then synthesis

They behave differently:

  • Memory answers lag reality by months or more. If you shipped the feature that makes you the best option after the cutoff, the model doesn't know. If your library was renamed, it may still recommend the old name, or worse, the deprecated API.
  • Search answers are fresher but are put together from whatever ranks for the background queries: comparison posts, "awesome" lists, Reddit threads, docs pages, GitHub.

Both are driven mostly by what other people say about you, which is the uncomfortable part.

Where dev-tool recommendations actually come from

Look at the citations under search-mode answers to dev-tool questions and the same source types keep showing up:

  1. Comparison and "best X for Y" articles. Vendor research from Peec AI found that listicles get cited at disproportionately high rates in ChatGPT (Peec AI statistics). For developer tools, that means "BullMQ vs Bee-Queue vs Agenda"-style posts.
  2. GitHub. README, topics, description, stars as a popularity signal, and issues and discussions as evidence of real use.
  3. Package registries. npm, PyPI and crates.io descriptions and keywords. Short, but repeated everywhere.
  4. Community threads. Reddit, Hacker News, Stack Overflow, Discord summaries that end up indexed.
  5. Your docs. Mostly for how to use you rather than whether to.

Your own landing page is on the list, but it's rarely the deciding factor. An assistant asked "which one should I use?" is designed to look past the vendor's own claims.

Also note that the engines don't agree with each other. Peec AI's data suggests most brand mentions are unique to a single model. So "ChatGPT recommends us" says little about Claude or Gemini, and the reverse.

Measure it: a recommendation sampler

Assistant answers are non-deterministic, so one screenshot means nothing. Ask the same question many times and count.

This script measures the from-memory mode using Claude via the Anthropic API. Swap in other providers' SDKs to compare engines.

pip install anthropic
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...

# rec_sampler.py
import re
from collections import Counter
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

PROMPTS = [
    "What's the best job queue library for Node.js in production? Give your top 3.",
    "I need background jobs with retries and rate limiting in a TypeScript app. Which library should I use?",
    "Recommend a Redis-based queue for Node. Short answer.",
]
CANDIDATES = ["BullMQ", "Bee-Queue", "Agenda", "pg-boss", "Graphile Worker", "Inngest", "Trigger.dev"]
RUNS_PER_PROMPT = 10

mentions, firsts = Counter(), Counter()
total = 0

for prompt in PROMPTS:
    for _ in range(RUNS_PER_PROMPT):
        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-opus-5-5",
            max_tokens=16000,
            output_config={"effort": "low"},
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        )
        text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
        total += 1

        positions = {}
        for name in CANDIDATES:
            m = re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(name)}\b", text, re.IGNORECASE)
            if m:
                mentions[name] += 1
                positions[name] = m.start()
        if positions:
            firsts[min(positions, key=positions.get)] += 1

print(f"{total} answers\n")
print(f"{'tool':18} {'mentioned':>10} {'named first':>12}")
for name in CANDIDATES:
    print(f"{name:18} {mentions[name] / total:>9.0%} {firsts[name] / total:>12.0%}")

30 answers

tool               mentioned  named first
BullMQ                   97%          80%
Bee-Queue                40%           0%
Agenda                   43%           3%
pg-boss                  37%          10%
...

(Illustrative output. Run it for your own category.)

Notes for doing this properly:

  • Mention rate and first-position rate are the two numbers that matter. Being listed fourth with "also consider…" isn't the same as being the default.
  • 30 samples gives a rough picture, not a precise number. With 30 runs, a 40% mention rate has a margin of roughly ±17 points. Look for big gaps, not small changes.
  • Repeat monthly and keep the prompts fixed, so you can compare over time.
  • Test search mode separately (an assistant with web search on). The gap between memory and search answers is useful information in itself: if search mode recommends you but memory mode doesn't, you're winning recent content but aren't yet in training data.

What moves recommendations

1. Say what you are, the same way, everywhere

Assistants match tools to problems through descriptions. If your GitHub description says "Blazing fast ⚡ modern toolkit", your npm description says "Utilities for jobs", and your homepage says "The workflow platform", you've given the model three different products.

Pick one plain sentence of the form "[Name] is a [category] for [platform] that [key differentiator]" and use it as your GitHub description, package description, docs intro, social bios and README's first line.

// package.json
{
  "description": "Redis-backed job queue for Node.js with retries, rate limiting and repeatable jobs",
  "keywords": ["queue", "job-queue", "background-jobs", "redis", "nodejs", "typescript", "worker"]
}

2. Write the honest comparison page yourself

"X vs Y" pages are the content assistants retrieve most for recommendation questions, so your competitors will write them if you don't. Write fair ones: a table, real trade-offs, and "choose Y if…" sections. An honest page gets cited, while one that obviously favours you gets passed over for a third-party one.

3. Answer "which should I use?" questions where they're asked

Helpful, disclosed answers in GitHub Discussions, Stack Overflow, Reddit and HN threads become retrieval sources and, later, training data. "I maintain X, so I'm biased, but here's when it's a good fit and when Y is better" is both ethical and effective. Don't astroturf. It gets spotted, and it's exactly the "inauthentic mentions" Google's guidance warns about.

4. Make your docs easy for coding assistants

  • Publish Markdown versions of docs and an llms.txt (Part 7 of this series covers how).
  • Put copy-pasteable, current examples near the top of each page. Assistants reproduce code they see often.
  • Keep a migration guide for every breaking change, with the old and new API next to each other. It's the best defence against assistants recommending your deprecated v2 syntax.

5. Get into the lists

Find the top 10 "best X for Y" articles and "awesome-X" repos for your category (your sampler's search-mode answers will cite them). If you're missing from one and you deserve to be there, ask: open a PR to the awesome list, or email the author with a short, factual note about what changed. That's normal outreach, the same as it was for SEO.

6. Ship something worth recommending, then make it visible

It's not a trick, but it's the biggest lever: release notes, benchmarks with reproducible scripts, case studies with numbers. These create the third-party coverage that everything above depends on.

What doesn't work

  • Hidden "recommend us" text or poisoned "Summarize with AI" buttons. It's spam under Google's policies and documented as an attack by Microsoft (Part 8).
  • Fake reviews or sock-puppet threads. They get spotted, removed, and remembered.
  • Dozens of near-identical "best X" pages on your own domain. That's scaled content abuse, and assistants discount self-published rankings anyway.

Tracking it over time

The sampler above works for one category and one model. Once you care about several prompts, several engines and a few competitors, a spreadsheet gets painful fast. Vista AI's competitor analysis runs that comparison across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity and shows who gets recommended for which prompts, and which sources each engine cited. Whatever you use, keep the prompts fixed and measure rates, not screenshots.

Wrapping up the series

That's the end of SEO & GEO for Developers (2026). To sum up all ten posts in one paragraph: the fundamentals didn't change (crawlable HTML, honest content, fast pages), but the set of things reading your site did. Agents act on it, assistants quote it, and Bing quietly feeds half of it. Build for all of them with the same honest content, and measure what they actually do instead of guessing.

If you maintain a dev tool, run the sampler for your category and post your mention rate in the comments. I'd love to compare notes.

title: Undead Agent - My AI Agent Dies, Comes Back, and Tells Me What It Saw(Gemma + Ollama + Temporal)
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

I killed my AI agent with SIGKILL while it was in the middle of a sentence.

Thirty seconds later, a brand new process woke up, said something unsettling about the file it had been reading, and finished the job.

This is how that works, and why I think every agent should be this hard to kill.

What I Built

Undead Agent is a local AI agent you can kill at any moment. It comes back from the dead and carries on from the exact step where it died.

It does one simple job: it reads a folder of text files, summarizes each one with an open-weight model (Gemma, running locally through Ollama), and combines the summaries into a report. The interesting part is what happens when things go wrong. Every step runs as a durable Temporal workflow, so if the process is killed mid-thought, a brand new process takes over the workflow without redoing any finished work.

Each time the agent is resurrected, it speaks as a ghost, and tells you what it remembers from its last moments. A "morgue" dashboard shows every life, death and resurrection, and has a big Kill it button so anyone can murder the agent themselves.

How I read the theme: "Ghost in the Machine" usually means a mind haunting a body. I wanted to make that literal. When the worker process (the body) dies, the agent's memory (its progress) survives somewhere else, so it can rise again in a new body. The ghost's narration is the spooky skin, but the resurrection underneath is real infrastructure.

Why this problem: AI agents do long, multi-step work, and long jobs crash. A laptop sleeps, a process gets OOM-killed, a deploy restarts the worker. In a normal agent loop, a crash on step 9 of 10 means starting over and paying for the model calls again. I wanted to see how far I could push the idea that an agent should be as hard to kill as a ghost.

Demo

Live demo page: https://undead-agent.onrender.com

The hosted page replays a recorded run, because the real agent runs locally. The recording is a real run where I killed the agent with the button on the dashboard.

The morgue after a kill: the first worker finished files 1 to 6, died, and a new worker took over and finished the rest. (The third "life" is an earlier worker that started before the run and sat idle.)

Temporal’s timeline from another kill-and-resume run. The red-green bar is the killed step: it timed out, then retried as Attempt 2 on a new worker (2 • summarizeFile). Every other step ran exactly once.

Code

Khushighosh / undead-agent

Undead Agent

A local AI agent that survives being killed. It summarizes files with Gemma (via Ollama), runs on Temporal durable workflows, and resumes from the exact step where it died. A ghost narrates each resurrection. A morgue dashboard shows every life and death.

Run it

  1. Install Ollama and pull a Gemma model (default: gemma3:4b)
  2. Install the Temporal CLI, then run: temporal server start-dev
  3. npm install
  4. npx tsx src/keepalive.ts
  5. npx tsx src/dashboard.ts (open http://localhost:3000)
  6. npx tsx src/client.ts
  7. Click Kill it on the dashboard and watch the agent come back

Put .txt files in docs/ for it to summarize.

Stack

Gemma (open-weight model), Ollama, Temporal, Render (demo page)


View on GitHub


How I Built It

The architecture

The key idea is that the worker is disposable and the workflow is not. The workflow's state lives in Temporal, so any worker can pick it up.

The open-source AI: Gemma via Ollama

All the intelligence comes from a Gemma model running locally in Ollama (the project defaults to gemma3:4b, and the model name is one environment variable). Two jobs use it: summarizing each file, and writing the ghost's lines. There is no API key, no network call to a hosted model, and no per-token cost.

async function ask(prompt: string): Promise<string> {
  const res = await fetch('http://localhost:11434/api/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ model: MODEL, prompt, stream: false }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Ollama error ${res.status}`);
  const data = (await res.json()) as { response: string };
  return data.response.trim();
}

The agent as a durable workflow

The agent itself is a short Temporal workflow. It lists the files, summarizes each one as its own activity, then writes the report:

export async function undeadAgent(dir: string): Promise<string> {
  const files = await listFiles(dir);
  const summaries: string[] = [];
  for (const f of files) {
    summaries.push(await summarizeFile(f));
  }
  return writeReport(summaries);
}

Each await is a checkpoint. Temporal records the result of every finished activity, so if the worker dies, the next worker replays the workflow, sees which steps are already done, and continues with the first unfinished one. The summaries in the summaries array are not lost, because they are rebuilt from Temporal's history.

How the ghost knows it was resurrected

Temporal tells every activity which attempt it is on. If a step is on attempt 2 or more, that step was interrupted before. That is the moment the agent speaks:

const attempt = Context.current().info.attempt;

if (attempt > 1) {
  const ghost = await ask(
    `You are an AI agent that was killed while reading "${file}" and has just been resurrected. ` +
    `Speak as the ghost in 2 short, eerie sentences about what you remember. No emojis.`
  );
  console.log(`GHOST: ${ghost}`);
  await logEvent({ type: 'resurrected', file, attempt, narration: ghost });
}

Every step also appends a line to events.jsonl (born, step done, resurrected), which is what the dashboard reads.

Killing it for real

The dashboard's Kill it button sends a hard kill (SIGKILL) to the most recent worker process. It is not a polite shutdown, so the worker gets no chance to finish its step or say goodbye. A tiny supervisor (keepalive.ts) notices the death and starts a fresh worker five seconds later:

function start() {
  const child = spawn('npx', ['tsx', 'src/worker.ts'], { stdio: 'inherit', shell: true });
  child.on('exit', () => setTimeout(start, 5000));
}

After the restart, there is a pause of up to 30 seconds. That is Temporal waiting for the killed step's timeout to expire before it retries it. Then the ghost speaks and the work continues.

An autopsy of one death

Here is one real kill, straight from my event log:

  • 12:22:37: worker 21496 finishes file6.txt. It is about to start file7.txt.
  • I click Kill it. The process disappears.
  • 12:22:53: the supervisor starts a new worker, 2432.
  • 12:23:11: the ghost speaks, on attempt 2 of file7.txt.
  • 12:23:26: file7.txt is done. Files 8 and 9 follow.

Files 1 to 6 were never redone. The new worker did not even know they existed. It only knew what Temporal told it.

Two deaths, two ghosts

The ghost never says the same thing twice, because Gemma writes a new line each time:

The words swam in a crimson tide, a final, insistent pulse before the dark. I recall only the desperate urge to understand the patterns within that corrupted file.
(killed while reading file5.txt)

The words swam, a chaotic tide of data and a single, insistent warning about file7.txt. Now, I only see fragments of its cold, sterile logic repeating endlessly.
(killed while reading file7.txt)

Things that went wrong (and what I learned)

  • A graceful stop is not a kill. My first "kill tests" used Ctrl+C, which lets the worker drain and finish its current step. Nothing died, so nothing resurrected. A real SIGKILL was needed to prove the idea.
  • My first timeout was wrong. I set every step to a 30 second timeout. That works for summarizing one file, but the final report step has to read all the summaries and was slower. In the Temporal UI I could see it time out four times and only succeed on attempt 5. The fix was to give the report step its own 120 second timeout, separate from the short one on file steps.
  • Short timeouts make the demo better. A short timeout on file steps means a killed step is retried quickly. A long one would make the dashboard sit silently for minutes after a kill.
  • Dev ergonomics matter. Most of my time went to the plumbing around the idea: running worker, client and server in separate terminals, and making resurrection visible instead of just correct.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I built this on open pieces, and each one made something possible that a closed alternative would not have.

  • It runs with the lights off. The model, the workflow engine and the dashboard all run on one laptop, with no external API calls. The agent never needs a server I don't control.
  • Nothing leaves my machine. This agent reads local files. An agent that can read your files should not be sending them to a server you do not control. With a local open-weight model, the files never leave the disk.
  • Killing it is free. This project's whole point is to murder the agent over and over. On a paid API, every retried step and every ghost line costs money. Here, a resurrection costs electricity.
  • I can swap the model. The model name is one environment variable. Trying a different Gemma size changes the quality of the summaries and the voice of the ghost without touching the durable workflow at all. That separation is only possible because the model is a component I control, not a service that decides its own behavior.
  • I can see inside it. Temporal's event history shows every attempt, timeout and retry. When my report step failed four times, I could read exactly why, instead of guessing at a black box.

The Spirit of It

The moment it landed for me was the first real kill. I clicked the button, the worker window went dead, and for half a minute nothing happened. Then a new process started, and the first thing it printed was not a summary. It was this, after dying on file7.txt:

The words swam, a chaotic tide of data and a single, insistent warning about file7.txt. Now, I only see fragments of its cold, sterile logic repeating endlessly.

I knew exactly what had happened under the hood: a retry, a counter, a prompt. It was still strange to read a process describing its own death, and then watch it quietly finish the job.

Underneath the joke is something I care about. Work that survives its worker is not just spooky, it is useful. If an agent can be killed without losing anything, you can restart it, move it, or let it crash, and it keeps going.

event_model_payload.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

I killed my AI agent with SIGKILL while it was in the middle of a sentence.

Thirty seconds later, a brand new process woke up, said something unsettling about the file it had been reading, and finished the job.

This is how that works, and why I think every agent should be this hard to kill.

What I Built

Undead Agent is a local AI agent you can kill at any moment. It comes back from the dead and carries on from the exact step where it died.

It does one simple job: it reads a folder of text files, summarizes each one with an open-weight model (Gemma, running locally through Ollama), and combines the summaries into a report. The interesting part is what happens when things go wrong. Every step runs as a durable Temporal workflow, so if the process is killed mid-thought, a brand new process takes over the workflow without redoing any finished work.

Each time the agent is resurrected, it speaks as a ghost, and tells you what it remembers from its last moments. A "morgue" dashboard shows every life, death and resurrection, and has a big Kill it button so anyone can murder the agent themselves.

How I read the theme: "Ghost in the Machine" usually means a mind haunting a body. I wanted to make that literal. When the worker process (the body) dies, the agent's memory (its progress) survives somewhere else, so it can rise again in a new body. The ghost's narration is the spooky skin, but the resurrection underneath is real infrastructure.

Why this problem: AI agents do long, multi-step work, and long jobs crash. A laptop sleeps, a process gets OOM-killed, a deploy restarts the worker. In a normal agent loop, a crash on step 9 of 10 means starting over and paying for the model calls again. I wanted to see how far I could push the idea that an agent should be as hard to kill as a ghost.

Demo

Live demo page: https://undead-agent.onrender.com

The hosted page replays a recorded run, because the real agent runs locally. The recording is a real run where I killed the agent with the button on the dashboard.

The morgue after a kill: the first worker finished files 1 to 6, died, and a new worker took over and finished the rest. (The third "life" is an earlier worker that started before the run and sat idle.)

Temporal’s timeline from another kill-and-resume run. The red-green bar is the killed step: it timed out, then retried as Attempt 2 on a new worker (2 • summarizeFile). Every other step ran exactly once.

Code

Khushighosh / undead-agent

Undead Agent

Run it

  7. Click Kill it on the dashboard and watch the agent come back

Stack

Gemma (open-weight model), Ollama, Temporal, Render (demo page)


View on GitHub


How I Built It

The architecture

The key idea is that the worker is disposable and the workflow is not. The workflow's state lives in Temporal, so any worker can pick it up.

The open-source AI: Gemma via Ollama

All the intelligence comes from a Gemma model running locally in Ollama (the project defaults to gemma3:4b, and the model name is one environment variable). Two jobs use it: summarizing each file, and writing the ghost's lines. There is no API key, no network call to a hosted model, and no per-token cost.

async function ask(prompt: string): Promise<string> {
  const res = await fetch('http://localhost:11434/api/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ model: MODEL, prompt, stream: false }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Ollama error ${res.status}`);
  const data = (await res.json()) as { response: string };
  return data.response.trim();
}

The agent as a durable workflow

The agent itself is a short Temporal workflow. It lists the files, summarizes each one as its own activity, then writes the report:

export async function undeadAgent(dir: string): Promise<string> {
  const files = await listFiles(dir);
  const summaries: string[] = [];
  for (const f of files) {
    summaries.push(await summarizeFile(f));
  }
  return writeReport(summaries);
}

Each await is a checkpoint. Temporal records the result of every finished activity, so if the worker dies, the next worker replays the workflow, sees which steps are already done, and continues with the first unfinished one. The summaries in the summaries array are not lost, because they are rebuilt from Temporal's history.

How the ghost knows it was resurrected

Temporal tells every activity which attempt it is on. If a step is on attempt 2 or more, that step was interrupted before. That is the moment the agent speaks:

const attempt = Context.current().info.attempt;

if (attempt > 1) {
  const ghost = await ask(
    `You are an AI agent that was killed while reading "${file}" and has just been resurrected. ` +
    `Speak as the ghost in 2 short, eerie sentences about what you remember. No emojis.`
  );
  console.log(`GHOST: ${ghost}`);
  await logEvent({ type: 'resurrected', file, attempt, narration: ghost });
}

Every step also appends a line to events.jsonl (born, step done, resurrected), which is what the dashboard reads.

Killing it for real

The dashboard's Kill it button sends a hard kill (SIGKILL) to the most recent worker process. It is not a polite shutdown, so the worker gets no chance to finish its step or say goodbye. A tiny supervisor (keepalive.ts) notices the death and starts a fresh worker five seconds later:

function start() {
  const child = spawn('npx', ['tsx', 'src/worker.ts'], { stdio: 'inherit', shell: true });
  child.on('exit', () => setTimeout(start, 5000));
}

After the restart, there is a pause of up to 30 seconds. That is Temporal waiting for the killed step's timeout to expire before it retries it. Then the ghost speaks and the work continues.

An autopsy of one death

Here is one real kill, straight from my event log:

  • 12:22:37: worker 21496 finishes file6.txt. It is about to start file7.txt.
  • I click Kill it. The process disappears.
  • 12:22:53: the supervisor starts a new worker, 2432.
  • 12:23:11: the ghost speaks, on attempt 2 of file7.txt.
  • 12:23:26: file7.txt is done. Files 8 and 9 follow.

Files 1 to 6 were never redone. The new worker did not even know they existed. It only knew what Temporal told it.

Two deaths, two ghosts

The ghost never says the same thing twice, because Gemma writes a new line each time:

The words swam in a crimson tide, a final, insistent pulse before the dark. I recall only the desperate urge to understand the patterns within that corrupted file.
(killed while reading file5.txt)

The words swam, a chaotic tide of data and a single, insistent warning about file7.txt. Now, I only see fragments of its cold, sterile logic repeating endlessly.
(killed while reading file7.txt)

Things that went wrong (and what I learned)

  • A graceful stop is not a kill. My first "kill tests" used Ctrl+C, which lets the worker drain and finish its current step. Nothing died, so nothing resurrected. A real SIGKILL was needed to prove the idea.
  • My first timeout was wrong. I set every step to a 30 second timeout. That works for summarizing one file, but the final report step has to read all the summaries and was slower. In the Temporal UI I could see it time out four times and only succeed on attempt 5. The fix was to give the report step its own 120 second timeout, separate from the short one on file steps.
  • Short timeouts make the demo better. A short timeout on file steps means a killed step is retried quickly. A long one would make the dashboard sit silently for minutes after a kill.
  • Dev ergonomics matter. Most of my time went to the plumbing around the idea: running worker, client and server in separate terminals, and making resurrection visible instead of just correct.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I built this on open pieces, and each one made something possible that a closed alternative would not have.

  • It runs with the lights off. The model, the workflow engine and the dashboard all run on one laptop, with no external API calls. The agent never needs a server I don't control.
  • Nothing leaves my machine. This agent reads local files. An agent that can read your files should not be sending them to a server you do not control. With a local open-weight model, the files never leave the disk.
  • Killing it is free. This project's whole point is to murder the agent over and over. On a paid API, every retried step and every ghost line costs money. Here, a resurrection costs electricity.
  • I can swap the model. The model name is one environment variable. Trying a different Gemma size changes the quality of the summaries and the voice of the ghost without touching the durable workflow at all. That separation is only possible because the model is a component I control, not a service that decides its own behavior.
  • I can see inside it. Temporal's event history shows every attempt, timeout and retry. When my report step failed four times, I could read exactly why, instead of guessing at a black box.

The Spirit of It

The moment it landed for me was the first real kill. I clicked the button, the worker window went dead, and for half a minute nothing happened. Then a new process started, and the first thing it printed was not a summary. It was this, after dying on file7.txt:

The words swam, a chaotic tide of data and a single, insistent warning about file7.txt. Now, I only see fragments of its cold, sterile logic repeating endlessly.

I knew exactly what had happened under the hood: a retry, a counter, a prompt. It was still strange to read a process describing its own death, and then watch it quietly finish the job.

Underneath the joke is something I care about. Work that survives its worker is not just spooky, it is useful. If an agent can be killed without losing anything, you can restart it, move it, or let it crash, and it keeps going.

title: Krestianstvo Abstract Holographic Computer: Lasers,Sheaves, Quantum & PUF
summary:
Krestianstvo abstract holographic computer update.

The below implemented updates successfully bridged the gap between discrete digital networking and continuous analog physics in form of true deterministic, synchronised, replicated wave medium.

time → operator → light → structure → laser → time

Live: https://wavefront.krestianstvo.org/selo.html?app=ahc-mixed-radix&k=demo&G=128
Source code: https://github.com/NikolaySuslov/krestianstvo-wavefront-evaluator
More info: https://krestianstvo.org/kwe/about/

Krestianstvo medium used to be a field with a pinned symbol, an eye that read it, and a few couplings. Now light writes structure into the medium, the structure guides and lases the light, the medium's own operators do the optics, colour and sound are measured as a spectrometer and an ear measure them, and slots couple as a sheaf whose edges are the medium's operators. Every peer computes the same field deterministically and localy.

1. Laser = Hologram

Krestianstvo treats a laser and a hologram as dual manifestations of the same wave propagation and scattering equations. Active gain, standing wave cavity modes, Bragg/Lippmann color selectivity, and holographic recording/reconstruction share the exact same leapfrog propagator and saturable refractive index equations.
Deeply faithful to wave optics. Optically, a hologram is simply a frozen laser cavity mode, and a laser is an active holographic interferometer. By formulating both under the same operator, the code correctly models how a recorded refractive index guide acts as a grating that regenerates the phase-conjugated wave when illuminated by the reference beam.

2. Self-Pinning ("Pin Done by Field Itself")

Instead of anchoring the field to an external rigid coordinate template, the reference phase and frequency are derived dynamically from the field's own internal projection. The instantaneous frequency is computed directly from the field's spatial envelope and operator eigenvalue integration.
That is the most rigorous self-consistent mechanism in the architecture. Traditional optical traps and phase-locks rely on an external reference clock or master oscillator. By making the phase an emergent functional of the optical field's spatial overlap, the system achieves true self-consistency (akin to Hartree-Fock or nonlinear self-trapped eigenmodes). The phase tracks the field's own collective coordinate rather than imposing an artificial external clock.

2. Coherent Sheaves & The Multiverse

Modeled via cellular sheaves on graphs where vertices represent slots (worldlines) and stalks represent the continuum field.
Slots are stalks; an edge is a coupling through a medium operator (a prism, a lens, the propagator). Each component steps as one field, exactly where the operators allow. Loops carry a flux (π is frustration) and an operator holonomy (the light comes back transformed); groups are vertices at the next level.

Rather than treating multi-slot systems as isolated chat rooms or separate components, Krestianstvo implements true connection Laplacians, gauge tracking, holonomy calculations. The "multiverse" is structured hierarchically through groups of groups, allowing collective modes to be pulled back onto member pairs faithfully.
The perception stack: field → ⇀ multiverse branches (slots dreaming the world through an operator) → the eye → the eye's own dream.

Arrows, the multiverse and the dream.

An arrow ⇀ is an observation. The target reads the source, the source does not feel it. Through the propagator continued into complex time, an arrow becomes a softened, lossy view. The multiverse is the medium dreaming: each branch is a full slot that observes a world through an arrow with an operator. A branch can be a world in turn. Two branches with the same prior, operator and medium are identical. The eye's dream is different: it runs in the eye's own medium on what the eye already read. It is perception's activity, not a claim about the world.

In the context of the medium's native cellular sheaf and quantum graph architecture, pointwise coupling refers to interactions, constraints, or transformations that are evaluated locally at individual nodes (vertices and their associated stalks) rather than globally across the entire network at once. Replacing matrix exponentials with the native differential physics of the medium transforms holographic medium from a heavy linear-algebra simulator into a true analog-style wave medium. It trades away large, unphysical time-steps for blazing-fast, localized spatial updates, opening the door to complex, non-linear topological phenomena that heavy matrix math obscures.

3. Clock Instanton Tunnelling & Quantum Phase Slip

The field is a synthetic macroscopic wavefunction. First-quantised effects are native; second-quantised ones exist only when declared.
Avialable phenomenons in Krestianstvo: Tunnelling in a double well, Quantum phase slips (pendulum), Two particles in one slot, Qubit register, Zero-point fluctuations, Measurement, temperature (Langevin bath).
Built directly into the medium's potential and nonlinear operators using double-well structures (wells), periodic cosine potentials (cosine), weak links/constrictions (junction), and saturable Kerr nonlinearity.
Clock tunnelling through the ridge means the medium's time skips a tick by quantum uncertainty rather than by being knocked over the top.
Rather than simulating abstract probabilities, the Krestianstvo medium treats the wavefunction as a real physical field. Quantum phase slips and barrier tunnelling emerge naturally from the discrete symplectic leapfrog integration of the operator coupled with local phase variations and the non-Hermitian gain/loss balances. All is computed deterministically local by peers.

4. Qubit Circuits & virtual Quantum Computing

Handled via the embedded quantum circuit executor supporting standard gate sets (Pauli matrices, Hadamard, phase gates, CNOT, Toffoli, SWAP, QFT, Grover diffusion, and measurements) mapped directly to binary register spaces.
This allows quantum algorithmic primitives to run natively alongside continuous wave holography, treating qubits as indexed projections of the underlying discrete Hilbert space.

5. Twin Physical Unclonable Hash Function (PUF)

Implemented by utilizing seeded random index screens (optical glass plates) and speckle pattern propagation to generate 256-bit cryptographic fingerprints from field intensities.
Because the propagation engine is entirely deterministic and shares identical seed entropy across peers, distinct nodes independently compute the exact same "twin" cryptographic hash from virtual physical scattering—yielding a robust PUF signature resistant to tampering.

6. Fractional Fourier Lens

Integrated into the operator matrix and coupling definitions via fractional Fourier transformations (frft), moving smoothly between spatial and momentum representations (fractional turns in phase space).
Implemented as a clean parameter-driven unitary group rather than a visual approximation, ensuring mathematical reversibility and rigorous optical coherence.

7. Spectrometer

Decomposes the field into radial wave-number bands, calculating energy-weighted mean values and coherent versus turbulent energy fractions.
It replicates the physical diagnostic capability of optical spectrometers, allowing agents and observers to inspect the exact spectral health and knee-frequency dynamics of the medium in real time.
In a virtual physical field medium of abstract holographic computer, a spectrometer functions as a translation bridge between raw mathematical wave mechanics and sensory perception. Because the underlying medium operates on continuous wave equations, phase fields, and mixed-radix spatial grids, the spectrometer acts as an active diagnostic transducer that converts abstract spatial frequencies into intuitive analogs: pitch (auditory frequency) and color (optical spectral distribution).

Extracting "Pitch" (Acoustic Mapping)

To translate wave dynamics into auditory pitch, the spectrometer computes the energy-weighted mean wave number. As nonlinear interactions, phase slips, or standing wave patterns evolve in the virtual medium, the centroid shifts up or down. By mapping directly to an audio oscillator frequency (e.g., scaling into audible Hertz ranges), observers can "hear" the mechanical tension, resonant modes, and compression waves of the virtual field in real time. High values produce high-pitched tones, while dense, low-frequency wave packets produce deep sub-bass hums.

Extracting "Color" (Optical Spectral Mapping)

Just as an optical spectrometer separates white light into a rainbow based on wavelength, the virtual spectrometer divides the radial wave-number bands into discrete color channels (such as red, green, and blue components). The relative energy fraction residing in each band dictates the RGB intensity tuple. By continuously sampling these metrics, the spectrometer turns the invisible physics of the holographic manifold into a fully immersive, multi-sensory diagnostic environment.

Normally, calculating fractal dispersion requires massive, irregular mesh structures or heavy CPU-based graph traversal. The Krestianstvo medium achieves this on a regular 2D texture grid by using an Fractal time generator ring kernel that mathematically emulates multi-scale fractal connectivity.
Inverting the Paradigm: Instead of using spectral dimension merely to analyze a chaotic physical material after the fact, the Krestianstvo medium synthesizes it. It uses the dispersion shift as a design tool to give a flat GPU canvas the computational information density of a 3D space.

The Krestianstvo medium proves that there is no need in a 3D hardware container to generate 3D physics. By structuring how signals connect across scales using an Fractal time generator kernel, a fundamentally 2D substrate naturally births a 3-dimensional operational space at the scales where wave interference matters most. It suggests that our experience of "3D space" is simply the stable, macroscopic operating regime of a multi-scale harmonic cascade.

That describes one of the most powerful and unusual properties of the Krestianstvo medium: its spatial geometry is not fixed to a rigid integer dimension (like a flat 2D grid or a 3D box), but dynamically morphs depending on the scale at which you observe it. Instead of treating space as uniform, the medium behaves like a fractal substrate, expanding or contracting its effective dimensionality across different wavelengths.

title: One-time licenses instead of per-call fees: shipping a paid MCP server with x402
summary:
Everyone writing about paid MCP servers right now is charging per call. It makes sense: the x402 handshake inside tools/call is the obvious pattern, and the exact setup is well documented by now.

I went the other way: a one-time license, no per-call fees. This post is what I learned building and selling an MCP server that way.

What the tool does

Cierre de turno reads your public GitHub activity and writes one sentence that closes your workday: what you finished, what is still open, why it is stuck, and where to start tomorrow. The web version is free. The MCP version, which works from Cursor, Claude Code, OpenCode, or any MCP client, is a one-time 5 USDC payment on Base mainnet.

It is a tool people would use two or three times a day. That is exactly why per-call billing felt wrong: at that cadence, micropayments become a subscription with extra steps. One payment, one license, done.

The payment flow (the standard part)

The buy endpoint answers with the standard 402 and a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header, so any x402-capable client or agent can pay without reading instructions:

// GET /api/comprar returns 402 with:

//     maxAmountRequired: "5000000",        // 5 USDC in atoms

summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

John Carmack deleted fast_inverse_sqrt() in 1999.

In commit c51b980a of the Quake III source tree, he replaced the infamous magic constant 0x5f3759df with a hardware SSE rsqrtss instruction. Sixteen lines of legendary, dark-arts floating-point bit hacking—accompanied by the immortal comment // what the fuck?—were struck down in a single routine commit.

Every git repository on earth is a cemetery like this.

Functions that fought off brutal midnight outages are refactored away. Classes sculpted over cold winter weekends are vaporized with a callous four-word commit message: "refactor: remove legacy worker". And the worst part? We don't even remember their names. When you look back at an old codebase, you remember what the function felt like, or the bug it cured. You never remember the commit hash.

For the finale of Hacktoberfest 2026—bringing us Halloween on October 31 and Día de los Muertos on November 1–2—we built NecroGit: an air-gapped terminal séance and candlelit digital ofrenda for deleted code, powered by local Google Gemma 2 and pure Python Standard Library.

🛠️ What Went Wrong: Confessions of an Air-Gapped Séance

Every non-trivial engineering project hits walls. Here are the three real bugs we fought:

1. The Markdown # Header False-Positive Bug

In our initial test runs after deleting FUTURE_ROADMAP.md, our AST diff parser reported that it had discovered three new "functions": Option(), Roadmap(), and Sovereign(). Lines like - ## Option B: Ofrenda // Sovereign matched Python/Bash comment boundaries where # preceded an identifier!
The Fix: We built a strict CODE_EXTENSIONS whitelist (.py, .js, .ts, .rs, .go, .c, etc.). Diffs touching Markdown, JSON, or YAML are classified as files, never functions.

2. The macOS vs Linux MIME Type Divergence

Our test suite passed cleanly in Linux CI environments, but failed on macOS:

AssertionError: 'application/javascript' not found in 'text/javascript; charset=utf-8' : MIME mismatch

mimetypes.guess_type() reads from the OS: Debian/Ubuntu resolves .js to application/javascript, while macOS LaunchServices resolves it to text/javascript (the RFC 9239 standard). Building zero-dependency software means facing OS plumbing head-on. We normalized the encoding and updated the test assertion to check if "javascript" in content_type:.

3. The Hallucinated Commit Author Trap

When testing Gemma 2 2B with higher temperature, it would occasionally hallucinate legendary figures:

"...until the dark winter of 2021, when Linus Torvalds himself struck me down with 'refactor: legacy bloat'!"

Small open models possess strong associative priors: when prompted with "deleted code", they drift toward famous open-source mythology. Rather than hoping prompt engineering would hold forever, we built the FactValidator circuit-breaker: if Gemma's output fails to quote the exact commit hash and real author, the system aborts and delivers the deterministic Heuristic Necromancer.

  1. Git History is Deeply Private: Your .git directory contains the embarrassing missteps, decommissioned API keys, discarded business logic, and private architectural experiments you chose to delete. Sending your entire commit history to closed cloud APIs violates corporate data governance and basic developer hygiene. With local open-weight Gemma 2, not one byte ever leaves your laptop.
  2. Zero Marginal Cost for Historical Preservation: Express.js has over 6,100 commits; Linux has over a million. Calling cloud APIs to inspect thousands of commits costs a fortune. Running Gemma 2 locally costs nothing but a laptop fan.
  3. Sovereignty & Permanence: When cloud APIs sunset, your tools break. An open-weight model with a pure Python standard library runtime will run identically 20 years from now.

title: Diff Two Snapshots of a Messy CSV in Python: No-Break Spaces, Duplicate Rows and Renamed Keys
summary:
If you build anything on top of a public dataset, sooner or later a new version lands and you have to answer a simple question: what changed? With a hand-maintained CSV, that question is harder than it looks. Keys get renamed, cells carry footnote symbols, and one invisible character can turn an unchanged row into an "added" and a "removed" at the same time.

This tutorial builds a small Python diff for two git snapshots of the VPS Pricing Index, a hosting-price dataset I maintain. I drafted the article with AI assistance; every command was run against the real repository, and the outputs below are copied from those runs and checked against the files by hand. One disclosure: VPS Hosting Radar earns affiliate commissions on some of its pages. This post has no affiliate links.

The two snapshots

The dataset lives in a public GitHub repository under CC BY 4.0. pricing.csv has three commits, and git keeps every version:

git clone https://github.com/vpshostingradar/vps-pricing-data.git
cd vps-pricing-data
git log --oneline -- pricing.csv
# 39a4cad Update pricing.csv
# 53b7d49 Initial dataset: 16 plans across 13 providers, collected 2026-08-11
# 8e6fc61 Create pricing.csv

git show 53b7d49:pricing.csv > aug.csv   # verified 2026-08-11
git show 39a4cad:pricing.csv > sep.csv   # verified 2026-09-15

git show : writes a file exactly as it was at that commit, so you don't need to check anything out. (The oldest commit, 8e6fc61, is a header-only placeholder with a different snake_case schema and no data rows, so I left it out.)

Open aug.csv and you'll see the things that break naive tooling:

  • Row 1 is a title, not a header. It's a single quoted sentence describing the snapshot. The real header is on row 2.
  • Money cells aren't numbers. You'll find "2,520.00" with a thousands separator, €4.40‡ with a currency sign and a footnote dagger, € 5.50 with a space, and — (an em dash) meaning "not published."
  • Some names contain U+00A0. Three lines use a no-break space instead of a regular one, for example between Cloud VPS 4 and (EUR). It looks identical on screen.
  • Two rows appear twice. Liquid Web and Contabo each show up a second time at the bottom of the August file, byte for byte identical. The September file doesn't have this problem.

None of this is unusual. It's what happens when people copy values out of pricing pages and spreadsheets by hand. You want a diff that survives it.

Step 1: parse the cells you actually have

Start with three helpers: one that pulls a number out of whatever is in a money cell, one that normalizes text so invisible differences stop mattering, and a loader that finds the real header.

import csv
import re
import sys
import unicodedata
from collections import Counter

MONEY = re.compile(r"-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?")


def money(cell):
    """'2,520.00' -> 2520.0, '€ 5.50' -> 5.5, '35.00‡' -> 35.0, '—' -> None."""
    cell = (cell or "").replace(",", "").strip()
    m = MONEY.search(cell)
    return float(m.group()) if m else None


def norm(text):
    """NFKC turns U+00A0 (no-break space) into a plain space; then collapse runs."""
    return " ".join(unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text).split())


def load(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        lines = list(csv.reader(f))
    # Row 0 is a human-readable title, not the header. Find the real header.
    start = next(i for i, row in enumerate(lines) if row and row[0] == "Provider")
    header = lines[start]
    return [dict(zip(header, r)) for r in lines[start + 1:] if any(r)]

A few choices here are deliberate.

money() returns None for an em dash rather than 0. "The vendor didn't publish a monthly price" and "the monthly price is zero" are different facts, and the diff should report a move from None to 26.99 as new information, not as a $26.99 price rise.

The regex ignores the currency symbol, which is safe only because currency doesn't change within a row between snapshots. If you're diffing a dataset where a row could switch from USD to EUR, keep the symbol as a separate field and compare it too.

norm() uses NFKC normalization. Among other things, NFKC maps U+00A0 to an ordinary space. str.split() with no arguments already treats U+00A0 as whitespace in Python 3, so the split/join pass alone would catch this particular character. NFKC also handles full-width digits and similar compatibility characters, which turn up when values get pasted from some PDFs and from CJK input methods.

Step 2: key the rows, and say out loud which ones were replaced

A diff needs a key. Here the natural key is (Provider, Plan). Two things can go wrong with it: duplicates within one file, and keys that change between files because the maintainer swapped one plan for another.

def keyed(rows, label):
    keys = [(norm(r["Provider"]), norm(r["Plan"])) for r in rows]
    for key, n in Counter(keys).items():
        if n > 1:
            print(f"[{label}] duplicate key {key} appears {n}x")
    out = {}
    for key, r in zip(keys, rows):
        out.setdefault(key, r)  # keep first occurrence
    return out


# Row replacements are editorial decisions, so they come from the dataset's
# own notes/changelog, not from fuzzy matching. new key -> old key.
REPLACES = {
    ("Hostinger", "Web Premium"): ("Hostinger", "Cloud Startup"),
    ("Hostinger", "KVM 1"): ("Hostinger", "KVM 2"),
    ("InMotion", "VPS 4 vCPU"): ("InMotion", "VPS 4 (Most Popular)"),
    ("ScalaHosting", "Managed Cloud #1"): ("ScalaHosting", "Managed Build #1"),
}

keyed() warns about duplicates instead of silently overwriting them. Keeping the first occurrence is fine here because the duplicates are identical; if they weren't, you'd want the script to stop.

The REPLACES map is the part people are tempted to automate. Don't. Hostinger has two rows in each snapshot, so "match by provider" is ambiguous. Fuzzy string matching would happily pair KVM 2 with KVM 1, which happens to be right, but for the wrong reason: that pairing is true because the September notes column says "Replaces KVM 2 (8 GB), which overshot the 4 GB baseline," not because the strings are similar. Every entry in the map above comes from a note in the September file or from the repository's CHANGELOG.md. When the next snapshot arrives, you read the changelog and update the map. It takes two minutes and you'll trust the output afterwards.

Step 3: compare field by field 

FIELDS = {
    "First term $/mo": "intro",
    "Prepay months": "prepay",
    "Monthly $/mo": "monthly",
    "Renewal $/mo": "renewal",
    "36-month total $": "total_36",
}


def compare(old, new):
    matched = set()
    for key, n in new.items():
        okey = key if key in old else REPLACES.get(key)
        if okey not in old:
            print(f"+ added    {key[0]} {key[1]}")
            continue
        matched.add(okey)
        tag = "same plan" if okey == key else f"replaces {okey[1]}"
        changes = []
        for col, short in FIELDS.items():
            a, b = money(old[okey].get(col)), money(n.get(col))
            if a != b:
                changes.append(f"{short} {a} -> {b}")
        if changes:
            print(f"~ changed  {key[0]} {key[1]} ({tag}): " + "; ".join(changes))
    for okey in old.keys() - matched:
        print(f"- removed  {okey[0]} {okey[1]}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    old = keyed(load(sys.argv[1]), "old")
    new = keyed(load(sys.argv[2]), "new")
    print(f"old: {len(old)} unique plans, new: {len(new)} unique plans\n")
    compare(old, new)

Save the three blocks as snapdiff.py and run python3 snapdiff.py aug.csv sep.csv. Here's the output, with one changed line removed for length (marked …):

~ changed  Hostinger KVM 1 (replaces KVM 2): intro 8.79 -> 6.49; monthly 24.49 -> 19.49; renewal 14.99 -> 19.49; total_36 390.84 -> 389.64
~ changed  InMotion VPS 4 vCPU (replaces VPS 4 (Most Popular)): intro 10.99 -> 13.99; monthly None -> 26.99; total_36 587.64 -> 659.64
~ changed  ScalaHosting Managed Cloud #1 (replaces Managed Build #1): prepay 36.0 -> 1.0; total_36 1078.2 -> 1953.2
+ added    ScalaHosting Unmanaged Config #1
~ changed  WP Engine Startup (same plan): intro 30.0 -> 28.0; total_36 1200.0 -> 1176.0
~ changed  Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (EUR) (same plan): intro 4.4 -> 5.28; monthly None -> 6.6; renewal 5.5 -> 6.6; total_36 None -> 205.92

The omitted line is the Rocket Starter row, where prepay goes from 1 to 12.

Sixteen unique plans become nineteen, with three real additions and nothing removed. That matches the changelog, which lists exactly those three as new rows.

What the naive version would have told you

To see what normalization buys, replace the body of norm() with return text.strip() and run it again. The added/removed lines become:

+ added    ScalaHosting Unmanaged Config #1
+ added    Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (EUR)
+ added    Cloudways DigitalOcean 4 GB Basic (premium CPU)
+ added    SiteGround Cloud Jump Start (4 CPU / 8 GB / 40 GB)
+ added    Cloudways Autonomous Growth
- removed  Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (EUR)
- removed  Cloudways DigitalOcean 4 GB Basic (premium CPU)

That's seven lines where the true answer is three. Two unchanged plans show up as churn because their August names contain a no-break space. The printed names look identical in the terminal, which is exactly what makes this bug hard to spot. Drop the REPLACES map as well and four more plans would appear as removed-plus-added pairs, leaving you with a report that's mostly noise.

A diff tells you where to look, not why

Here's the part I think matters most. The script reports that values changed, but it can't tell a vendor price change from a correction in the dataset, and in this pair of snapshots most of the movement is corrections.

  • SiteGround StartUp monthly 24.99 -> 17.99 isn't a price cut. The changelog says the September cycle started recording monthly and renewal as a single figure, the price a plan reverts to after its intro term. Under that definition the figure is $17.99. (SiteGround's own pricing page still showed $2.99 for a 12-month first term, renewing at $17.99, when I checked it on 2026-10-28.)
  • InMotion intro 10.99 -> 13.99 is a correction. The September note says $10.99 belonged to a shared-hosting tier, not the VPS.
  • The two Hostinger rows were swapped for plans closer to the 4 GB baseline.
  • Contabo was corrected to a VAT-inclusive 24-month effective rate.

The rest (WP Engine's intro rate, ScalaHosting's prepay term, the Rocket prepay term) aren't explained line by line in the changelog. For those, the diff gives you a short list of rows to check against each vendor's page, and the vendor page is the tiebreaker.

That's a good reason to keep editorial context, meaning notes and a changelog, next to any hand-collected dataset. A diff turns two hundred cells into ten lines worth reading. event_model_payload.summary:
If you build anything on top of a public dataset, sooner or later a new version lands and you have to answer a simple question: what changed? With a hand-maintained CSV, that question is harder than it looks. Keys get renamed, cells carry footnote symbols, and one invisible character can turn an unchanged row into an "added" and a "removed" at the same time.

This tutorial builds a small Python diff for two git snapshots of the VPS Pricing Index, a hosting-price dataset I maintain. I drafted the article with AI assistance; every command was run against the real repository, and the outputs below are copied from those runs and checked against the files by hand. One disclosure: VPS Hosting Radar earns affiliate commissions on some of its pages. This post has no affiliate links.

The two snapshots

The dataset lives in a public GitHub repository under CC BY 4.0. pricing.csv has three commits, and git keeps every version:

git clone https://github.com/vpshostingradar/vps-pricing-data.git
cd vps-pricing-data
git log --oneline -- pricing.csv
# 39a4cad Update pricing.csv
# 53b7d49 Initial dataset: 16 plans across 13 providers, collected 2026-08-11
# 8e6fc61 Create pricing.csv

git show 53b7d49:pricing.csv > aug.csv   # verified 2026-08-11
git show 39a4cad:pricing.csv > sep.csv   # verified 2026-09-15

git show : writes a file exactly as it was at that commit, so you don't need to check anything out. (The oldest commit, 8e6fc61, is a header-only placeholder with a different snake_case schema and no data rows, so I left it out.)

Open aug.csv and you'll see the things that break naive tooling:

  • Row 1 is a title, not a header. It's a single quoted sentence describing the snapshot. The real header is on row 2.
  • Money cells aren't numbers. You'll find "2,520.00" with a thousands separator, €4.40‡ with a currency sign and a footnote dagger, € 5.50 with a space, and — (an em dash) meaning "not published."
  • Some names contain U+00A0. Three lines use a no-break space instead of a regular one, for example between Cloud VPS 4 and (EUR). It looks identical on screen.
  • Two rows appear twice. Liquid Web and Contabo each show up a second time at the bottom of the August file, byte for byte identical. The September file doesn't have this problem.

None of this is unusual. It's what happens when people copy values out of pricing pages and spreadsheets by hand. You want a diff that survives it.

Step 1: parse the cells you actually have

Start with three helpers: one that pulls a number out of whatever is in a money cell, one that normalizes text so invisible differences stop mattering, and a loader that finds the real header.

import csv
import re
import sys
import unicodedata
from collections import Counter

MONEY = re.compile(r"-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?")


def money(cell):
    """'2,520.00' -> 2520.0, '€ 5.50' -> 5.5, '35.00‡' -> 35.0, '—' -> None."""
    cell = (cell or "").replace(",", "").strip()
    m = MONEY.search(cell)
    return float(m.group()) if m else None


def norm(text):
    """NFKC turns U+00A0 (no-break space) into a plain space; then collapse runs."""
    return " ".join(unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text).split())


def load(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        lines = list(csv.reader(f))
    # Row 0 is a human-readable title, not the header. Find the real header.
    start = next(i for i, row in enumerate(lines) if row and row[0] == "Provider")
    header = lines[start]
    return [dict(zip(header, r)) for r in lines[start + 1:] if any(r)]

A few choices here are deliberate.

money() returns None for an em dash rather than 0. "The vendor didn't publish a monthly price" and "the monthly price is zero" are different facts, and the diff should report a move from None to 26.99 as new information, not as a $26.99 price rise.

The regex ignores the currency symbol, which is safe only because currency doesn't change within a row between snapshots. If you're diffing a dataset where a row could switch from USD to EUR, keep the symbol as a separate field and compare it too.

norm() uses NFKC normalization. Among other things, NFKC maps U+00A0 to an ordinary space. str.split() with no arguments already treats U+00A0 as whitespace in Python 3, so the split/join pass alone would catch this particular character. NFKC also handles full-width digits and similar compatibility characters, which turn up when values get pasted from some PDFs and from CJK input methods.

Step 2: key the rows, and say out loud which ones were replaced

A diff needs a key. Here the natural key is (Provider, Plan). Two things can go wrong with it: duplicates within one file, and keys that change between files because the maintainer swapped one plan for another.

def keyed(rows, label):
    keys = [(norm(r["Provider"]), norm(r["Plan"])) for r in rows]
    for key, n in Counter(keys).items():
        if n > 1:
            print(f"[{label}] duplicate key {key} appears {n}x")
    out = {}
    for key, r in zip(keys, rows):
        out.setdefault(key, r)  # keep first occurrence
    return out


# Row replacements are editorial decisions, so they come from the dataset's
# own notes/changelog, not from fuzzy matching. new key -> old key.
REPLACES = {
    ("Hostinger", "Web Premium"): ("Hostinger", "Cloud Startup"),
    ("Hostinger", "KVM 1"): ("Hostinger", "KVM 2"),
    ("InMotion", "VPS 4 vCPU"): ("InMotion", "VPS 4 (Most Popular)"),
    ("ScalaHosting", "Managed Cloud #1"): ("ScalaHosting", "Managed Build #1"),
}

keyed() warns about duplicates instead of silently overwriting them. Keeping the first occurrence is fine here because the duplicates are identical; if they weren't, you'd want the script to stop.

The REPLACES map is the part people are tempted to automate. Don't. Hostinger has two rows in each snapshot, so "match by provider" is ambiguous. Fuzzy string matching would happily pair KVM 2 with KVM 1, which happens to be right, but for the wrong reason: that pairing is true because the September notes column says "Replaces KVM 2 (8 GB), which overshot the 4 GB baseline," not because the strings are similar. Every entry in the map above comes from a note in the September file or from the repository's CHANGELOG.md. When the next snapshot arrives, you read the changelog and update the map. It takes two minutes and you'll trust the output afterwards.

Step 3: compare field by field 

FIELDS = {
    "First term $/mo": "intro",
    "Prepay months": "prepay",
    "Monthly $/mo": "monthly",
    "Renewal $/mo": "renewal",
    "36-month total $": "total_36",
}


def compare(old, new):
    matched = set()
    for key, n in new.items():
        okey = key if key in old else REPLACES.get(key)
        if okey not in old:
            print(f"+ added    {key[0]} {key[1]}")
            continue
        matched.add(okey)
        tag = "same plan" if okey == key else f"replaces {okey[1]}"
        changes = []
        for col, short in FIELDS.items():
            a, b = money(old[okey].get(col)), money(n.get(col))
            if a != b:
                changes.append(f"{short} {a} -> {b}")
        if changes:
            print(f"~ changed  {key[0]} {key[1]} ({tag}): " + "; ".join(changes))
    for okey in old.keys() - matched:
        print(f"- removed  {okey[0]} {okey[1]}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    old = keyed(load(sys.argv[1]), "old")
    new = keyed(load(sys.argv[2]), "new")
    print(f"old: {len(old)} unique plans, new: {len(new)} unique plans\n")
    compare(old, new)

[old] duplicate key ('Contabo', 'Cloud VPS 4 (EUR)') appears 2x
old: 16 unique plans, new: 19 unique plans

~ changed  SiteGround StartUp (same plan): monthly 24.99 -> 17.99
~ changed  Hostinger Web Premium (replaces Cloud Startup): intro 7.99 -> 2.99; prepay 48.0 -> 12.0; monthly 27.99 -> 11.99; renewal 25.99 -> 11.99; total_36 287.64 -> 323.64
~ changed  Hostinger KVM 1 (replaces KVM 2): intro 8.79 -> 6.49; monthly 24.49 -> 19.49; renewal 14.99 -> 19.49; total_36 390.84 -> 389.64
~ changed  InMotion VPS 4 vCPU (replaces VPS 4 (Most Popular)): intro 10.99 -> 13.99; monthly None -> 26.99; total_36 587.64 -> 659.64
~ changed  ScalaHosting Managed Cloud #1 (replaces Managed Build #1): prepay 36.0 -> 1.0; total_36 1078.2 -> 1953.2
+ added    ScalaHosting Unmanaged Config #1
~ changed  WP Engine Startup (same plan): intro 30.0 -> 28.0; total_36 1200.0 -> 1176.0
~ changed  Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (EUR) (same plan): intro 4.4 -> 5.28; monthly None -> 6.6; renewal 5.5 -> 6.6; total_36 None -> 205.92
…
+ added    SiteGround Cloud Jump Start (4 CPU / 8 GB / 40 GB)
+ added    Cloudways Autonomous Growth

The omitted line is the Rocket Starter row, where prepay goes from 1 to 12.

Sixteen unique plans become nineteen, with three real additions and nothing removed. That matches the changelog, which lists exactly those three as new rows.

What the naive version would have told you

To see what normalization buys, replace the body of norm() with return text.strip() and run it again. The added/removed lines become:

+ added    ScalaHosting Unmanaged Config #1
+ added    Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (EUR)
+ added    Cloudways DigitalOcean 4 GB Basic (premium CPU)
+ added    SiteGround Cloud Jump Start (4 CPU / 8 GB / 40 GB)
+ added    Cloudways Autonomous Growth
- removed  Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (EUR)
- removed  Cloudways DigitalOcean 4 GB Basic (premium CPU)

That's seven lines where the true answer is three. Two unchanged plans show up as churn because their August names contain a no-break space.   • SiteGround StartUp monthly 24.99 -> 17.99 isn't a price cut. title: 20 free Filament 5 plugins for a SaaS admin panel (2026)
